content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes MAT (mixtured-strategy game of adversarial training). The idea is to formulate adversarial training as a mixed-strategy game instead of a pure-strategy game. The authors propose to use mirror descent to solve such a mixed-strategy game. Experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

* The idea of formulating adversarial training as a mixed-strategy game is very interesting. 

* The authors explained mixed-strategy games well.


Weaknesses:

* Presentation of the paper needs to improve. 

  * I suggest moving Section 3.2 to the related work or background section. This subsection is simply an introduction to mixed-strategy games and has nothing to do with the proposed algorithm.

  * Some notations should be changed. For example, $\Delta$ is used to denote a probability simplex in Section 3.2, which I do not think is the case in $\delta \in\ Delta$ (e.g., Eq. 6). Also, Eq. 9 is an approximation to Eq. 8, so the RHS in Eq. 8 and Eq. 9 are not equal.

* Some claims in the paper seem rather arbitrary. For example, in the abstract, the authors claim that “previous adversarial training methods suffer from converging onto local optima due to the non-convexity of the objective“. However, no theoretical results are given regarding convexity of the new training objective. Also, correct me if I’m wrong, but I do not think the proposed method can resolve the “local optimality” issue (if this is even an issue). 

* Complexity of the proposed algorithm seems rather high according to Algorithm 2. Specifically, in each training iteration, the algorithm needs to calculate $2K$ gradients, whereas conventional adversarial training only needs to calculate $K$ gradients. The authors should provide empirical results on the training speed.

* Another concern is about experiments.

  * The authors conducted experiments on the GLUE benchmark but left out the two largest datasets: QQP and MNLI. In general, MNLI is considered the most representative task in GLUE, because smaller datasets are more sensitive to hyper-parameter tuning. The authors should include results on QQP and MNLI. The authors mentioned “we abandoned training MNLI and QQP, because their size is too big“. This is not a valid excuse since even MNLI only contains 400k training samples.

  * The authors left out an important baseline [1], which is another game-motivated adversarial training approach. The proposed method (MAT) has lower accuracy than [1] on SST-2 and QNLI, which are magnitudes larger than the other datasets in which MAT outperforms [1].  

[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04886


Questions:

* I do not fully understand why changing Eq. 9 to Eq. 10. Could the authors provide more explanations and motivations?

* Also, why use the exponential moving average in Eq. 10?
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Reviewer vqZv
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and address all concerns below.

- **Presentation of the paper needs to improve.**

  - **I suggest moving Section 3.2 to the related work or background section. This subsection is simply an introduction to mixed-strategy games and has nothing to do with the proposed algorithm.**

    In Section 3.2 we provide scenarios and solutions for standard mixed strategy games, because we want the readers to read this paper smoothly without having to look at these prior knowledge from the appendix. And your suggestion will be duly considered.

  - **Some notations should be changed. For example, $Δ$ is used to denote a probability simplex in Section 3.2, which I do not think is the case in $δ∈ \Delta$ (e.g., Eq. 6). Also, Eq. 9 is an approximation to Eq. 8, so the RHS in Eq. 8 and Eq. 9 are not equal.**

    Thank you for your suggestion, we fixed this issue in the new version. But we keep the $\Delta$ unchanged, because the $\Delta$ before and after corresponds to different problem definitions, and usually both probability simplicity and disturbance are represented by $\Delta$. We are concerned that the use of the new notation definitions will confuse readers.

- **Some claims in the paper seem rather arbitrary.**

  We acknowledge that the expression of such motives is somewhat arbitrary. While it is true that mathematically the mixed-strategy finds the global optimum, we did not reach it when actually training the model. And we changed this statement in the new version.

- **Complexity of the proposed algorithm seems rather high according to Algorithm 2.**

  The complexity of our algorithm is indeed large, since MAT update the distribution of the model parameters in each iteration instead of a simple value. But you still underestimate the complexity of the algorithm. Adversarial training is usually 2 times more complex than fine-tuning training, and our algorithm is K times more complex than adversarial training.

- **Another concern is about experiments.**

  - **The authors conducted experiments on the GLUE benchmark but left out the two largest datasets: QQP and MNLI.**

    For large datasets, we think QNLI (100K) is enough to prove the effectiveness of our algorithm. And due to our lack of computational resources, it takes 6 days to train MNLI with MAT algorithm, so we gave up.

  - **The authors left out an important baseline [1], which is another game-motivated adversarial training approach.**

    Thank you for this suggestion. [1] is mentioned in the related work of our paper (Section 2.2). We did not select it as the baseline since our main reference is SMART. And we included it in the new version as our baseline.

- **I do not fully understand why changing Eq. 9 to Eq. 10. Could the authors provide more explanations and motivations?**

  In Eq. 9 we identified a batch of samples to estimate the distribution. But a problem is that we need to keep all the samples and compute the gradient on each sample. If we did this, the complexity of the algorithm would be $n'$ (number of samples) times the current complexity. So we simplified Eq. 9 to get Eq. 10, using the mean of the samples to estimate the distribution.

- **Also, why use the exponential moving average in Eq. 10?**

  Because in SGLD, it takes several iterations to converge, the later sample's are more reflective of the true distribution. Moving average helps us to adjust the weights of the samples collected in different periods.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper reformulate adversarial training in the view of mixed strategy in game theory and proposes mixed-strategy adversarial training (MAT). Specifically, this work use entropic mirror descent to find the mixed Nash Equilibria of the game. In practice, the authors uses stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics for implementation and use MAT to fine-tune several NLP models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The paper is easy to follow. Using mix-strategy formulation to solve adversarial training is new. Results on several tasks look promising.

Weakness:

1. Majority part of Section 3 is the same with "Hsieh et al (2019)", including using entropic mirror descent and calculating the update using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. The authors should clarify this to avoid misunderstanding.

2. In the formulation of (6), $\lambda$ is the coefficient controlling the trade-off between the clean accuracy $L(f_\theta(x), y)$ and the robust accuracy $L(f_\theta(x + \delta), y)$. Like in TRADES (Zhang et al, "Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness and accuracy". ICML 2019.), how to set $\lambda$ would be tricky. The authors should discuss about this.

3. Based on equations (13), $\theta_t$ and $\delta_t$ seem to be updated simultaneously. However, in the Algorithm 2, $\theta_t$ and $\delta_t$ are updated alternatively. The authors should explain the difference. I think, simultaneously updating the parameters have a guaranteed convergence while alternatively updating them usually has better performance.

4. It is possible to introduce the pre-conditioning in SGLD, the convergence guarantee still holds here. As far as I know, optimizers with conditioning, such as RMSprop and Adam, are broadly used in NLP tasks. In addition, unlike CV tasks, these methods with pre-conditioning usually have better performance in NLP tasks, especially for the architecture with recurrent connections.

5. The complexity of the algorithm is pretty high, because we need multiple steps for SGLD to converge.

6. For the experiments, the authors should compare the single strategy with MAT to demonstrate it is better to use mixed-strategy. In addition, as performances of some methods are quite similar, the authors should run the experiments for multiple times and report the variance.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and quality: this paper is generally well-written and easy to read. However, there are still some presentation mistakes.

* In equation (3), the function $F$ is not defined. I think $F(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \langle \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{B}\mathbf{q} \rangle - \langle \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{q} \rangle$.

* In Section 3.3, $l(P, Q) = \mathcal{D}_{KL} (P || Q) + \mathcal{D}\_{KL} (Q || P)$ is not the KL divergence between $P$ and $Q$ but two times the JS divergence between them.

Novelty: the novelty is not very high, as the majority part of Section 3 is similar to "Hsieh et al (2019)".

Reproducibility: The code is released, but I think the experiments in this work need to run multiple times and performance variance should be reported.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Based on the comments above, I cannot recommend this paper to publish in ICLR although it indeed introduces a framework and has some promising results.

I look forward to the discussion with the authors. I will re-evaluate this work if the authors can address my concerns.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Kiq7
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and address all concerns below.

1. **Majority part of Section 3 is the same with "Hsieh et al (2019)", including using entropic mirror descent and calculating the update using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. The authors should clarify this to avoid misunderstanding.**

   The MAT algorithm is indeed inspired by the paper you said, and we apply its approach of solving mixed-strategy games to adversarial training. In addition, since our starting point is different from that paper, our perturbation and model parameters are not equivalent like GAN, and we have done a lot of modification work on formula derivation, rather than simple transfer.

2. **In the formulation of (6), $λ$ is the coefficient controlling the trade-off between the clean accuracy $L(f_θ(x),y)$ and the robust accuracy $L(f_θ(x+δ),y)$.**

   Your understanding is correct, that $λ$ is indeed an important hyperparameter. And our setting of $λ$ follows the setting it in SMART, hyperparameters will be announced after final publication. Since the starting point of our objective function comes from a part of SMART, we do not think we need to repeat the discussion of the setting of $λ$ under the mixed strategy.

   SMART: Robust and Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-trained Natural Language Models through Principled Regularized Optimization (ACL 2020)

3. **Based on equations (13), $θ_t$ and $δ_t$ seem to be updated simultaneously. However, in the Algorithm 2, $θ_t$ and $δ_t$ are updated alternatively.**

   A misunderstanding arises here due to the fact that we have written the iterations of $θ_t$ and $δ_t$ together in Eq. (13). In fact, in Eq. (13), $θ_t$ and $δ_t$ are also updated alternately. In the adversarial training, the perturbation is the first party to move, so it updates its parameter first.

4. **It is possible to introduce the pre-conditioning in SGLD, the convergence guarantee still holds here.**
   
   The reason why we use SGLD is that we get the form of the final parameter distribution with MD. We will try the approach you mentioned in future study, but it may not help reduce the complexity of the algorithm.

5. **The complexity of the algorithm is pretty high, because we need multiple steps for SGLD to converge.**

   Yes, you are right. Updating a distribution is much more difficult than updating a value.

6. **For the experiments, the authors should compare the single strategy with MAT to demonstrate it is better to use mixed-strategy. In addition, as performances of some methods are quite similar, the authors should run the experiments for multiple times and report the variance.**

   We did compare with pure strategy approaches, such as FreeLB, SMART. Their methods of model parameter update are based on pure strategy. Reporting the variance is a useful suggestion, although some of our baselines alse do not report variance. And we aim to submit our variance data in the next version.

- **In equation (3), the function $F$ is not defined. I think $F(p,q)=⟨p,Bq⟩−⟨p,Aq⟩$.**

  There is nothing wrong with your understanding, but we actually talk about this abbreviation in the original paper. Just above the line of Eq (3), we write "**if we abbreviate Eq.2 with F**".

- **In Section 3.3, $l(P, Q) = D_{KL} (P || Q) + D_{KL} (Q || P)$ is not the KL divergence between $P$ and $Q$ but two times the JS divergence between them.**

  Sorry, we don't understand what you mean here. This definition refers to the original SMART paper and we did not make any changes. As for JS divergence, we find $J S\left(P_1 \| P_2\right)=\frac{1}{2} K L\left(P_1 \| \frac{P_1+P_2}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2} K L\left(P_2 \| \frac{P_1+P_2}{2}\right)$. Of course, this loss function $l(P, Q)$ can also be modified into other forms, we just refer to the original definition. If you have better suggestions, you can reply us again.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper models the fine-tuning adversarial training problem as a mixed-strategy game problem, and derived a strategy updating method to obtain Nash equilibrium solution of the problem. With some tricks to make the sampling subprocess feasible, and using the stochastic Langevin dynamics to perform the sampling, the proposed MAT algorithm can converge and be used to fine-tune a pertained model. Experiments on GLUE shows improvement using MAT over SOTA methods, and ANLI experiments show that MAT's robustness against adversarial samples are better than other methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
1. The idea is novel and interesting.
2. The derived algorithm to solve the MAT problem is also practical and easy to follow.
3. The performance on part of the benchmark dataset is promising.

Cons:
1. I am not sure about the motivation of viewing adversarial fine-tuning problem as a mixed-strategy game problem. In the abstract, the author states "However, from the perspective of optimization, the previous adversarial training methods suffer from converging onto local optima due to the non-convexity of the objective", but I don't see how the MAT framework solves the convexity problem, nor escaping the local optimal. The authors need to provide more explanations on the motivations. 
2. From equation 9 to 10, the approximation leads to significant variance. No analysis on the bound of errors so we don't know how far it converges to from the actual Nash equilibrium.
3. Unfortunately, the proposed method is too slow for practical usage. Fine-tuning process is meant to be fast and simple. If it is too slow to even cover some of the GLUE benchmark datasets, this significantly limit the usage of the algorithm.
4. Typos: page 4 at the top: p, q is represented -> p, q are representing

content.title: Response to Reviewer pwk7
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and address all concerns below.

1. **I am not sure about the motivation of viewing adversarial fine-tuning problem as a mixed-strategy game problem.**

   We acknowledge that the expression of such motives is somewhat arbitrary. While it is true that mathematically the mixed-strategy finds the global optimum, we did not reach it when actually training the model. And we will change this statement in the new version.

2. **From equation 9 to 10, the approximation leads to significant variance. No analysis on the bound of errors so we don't know how far it converges to from the actual Nash equilibrium.**

   When we thought of using samples to estimate the distribution, we realized that this would make the algorithm more complicated because we would need to perform a forward and backward propagation on each sample. So it would seem that using the mean of a set of samples is a simplified solution, but it is certain that it introduces variance you said.

3. **Unfortunately, the proposed method is too slow for practical usage. Fine-tuning process is meant to be fast and simple. If it is too slow to even cover some of the GLUE benchmark datasets, this significantly limit the usage of the algorithm.**

   The algorithmic complexity of MAT comes from updating the distribution of the model parameters rather than the value, which is the biggest advantage of the mixed strategy, so we have no way to solve it for the time being. Due to our lack of computational resources, it took 6 days to train MNLI with MAT, so we gave up. If the computing resources are sufficient, MAT can improve the model, so the actual usage scenarios still exist.

4. **Typos: page 4 at the top: p, q is represented -> p, q are representing**

   The original text is "each element in p, q is represented the probability of each pure strategy". The subject of this sentence is "each element", so we don't think any changes are needed here. If you still have concerns, you can respond to us again.

content.title: Response to Reviewer HQXQ
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback and address all concerns below.

- **The performance improvement is not very significant, and the algorithm results in significantly longer training time.**

  Referring to the results reported in previous papers, using the same pre-trained model but different fine-tuning methods, a 1% improvement in the GLUE benchmark can also be considered significant.  And the complexity of the algorithm comes from the fact that we update the distribution of the model parameters instead of a value, which is an important innovation point in our paper.

- **Missing an important reference.**

  The content of our paper is not relevant to the mentioned paper, where we focus on updating model parameters using the mixed-strategy when fine-tuning the pre-trained model, while the paper you mentioned focuses on training multiple classifier models with the mixed-strategy. That means we end up with a single model, while the paper you mentioned gets a combination of multiple models.

- **The adversarial perturbation is conducted on the embedding space. Since sentences are a sequence of words (i.e., discrete). Therefore, it may not be helpful in defending adversarial attacks. Is it possible to manipulate the words instead of embeddings?**

  Existing research has shown that perturbing the embedding space during adversarial training can improve model robustness, see [1] for details. And our experimental results on ANLI further validate this point. We guess the reason is that if you modify the word, after the word is transformed into a vector, there will be a difference between its vector and the original word vector in the embedding space, which we call a perturbation. But this perturbation is not essentially different from the perturbation that we add directly to the vector of the original word. There are also existing some methods for generating adversarial examples that directly perturb the embedding space and reverse the conversion to words. It should be further clarified that our study does not care how to generate perturbation or adversarial examples.

- **Eq. (6) is problematic. Why does the attacker use the same perturbation on all examples?**

  Eq. (6) comes from [1], and there are some misunderstandings here. It is certain that different examples correspond to different amounts of perturbation. In Eq. (6), $B$  is used to denote a batch. $B$ has a shape of $(batch\\_size, max\\_len, embed\\_dim)$, and $\delta$ has the same shape as $B$. Therefore, the 0th dimension of $\delta$ indicates the corresponding sample in $B$.

[1] SMART: Robust and Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-trained Natural Language Models through Principled Regularized Optimization (ACL 2020)
